The pups remain on the beach after weaning, fasting for several weeks while they complete their post-weaning development and learn to swim before departing to sea.

After this gestation period, females haul out on isolated insular and mainland beaches to give birth, typically within days of arrival. The timing of parturition is highly synchronized, with most births occurring between late December and early February across the species' range. Following the birth event, females enter a brief post-partum estrus and mate before departing to sea, leaving the pup to be weaned by the male-defended harem structure. This compressed reproductive schedule means that females must simultaneously support both a developing foetus in utero and the energetic demands of milk production for the current pup, a physiological feat that demands massive lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding foraging migrations.

The extended lifespan allows females to produce multiple offspring across their reproductive careers, each pup demanding the full annual investment of maternal resources. This life-history syndrome — large body size, long gestation, single offspring, extended lifespan — places the northern elephant seal among the most extreme mammalian examples of a slow-paced, K-selected reproductive strategy, perfectly adapted to the unpredictable pelagic environment they inhabit.
